pool.prompt: OPGW (Optical Ground Wire) is most commonly found on which type of structure?
choices: 40-ft joint-use distribution poles in residential neighborhoods — OPGW is not used there

High-voltage transmission towers, replacing the conventional overhead ground/shield wire at the very top of the structure, above all phase conductors — a transmission-structure product, not a distribution product
Underground handholes and vaults
Cellular tower guy wires
pool.explanation: OPGW replaces the conventional overhead ground/shield wire at the top of transmission towers (above all phase conductors), combining the lightning-shielding/fault-current function of a traditional shield wire with embedded optical fibers. It is fundamentally a transmission-structure product — a 40-ft joint-use distribution pole would use ADSS, lashed cable, or coax instead, not OPGW.

pool.prompt: Why must OPGW's metallic outer strands be sized to handle ground fault current, rather than just the mechanical load of supporting its own weight?
choices: To prevent aeolian vibration from damaging the fiber core — a different, unrelated failure mode

Because OPGW physically replaces the shield wire and inherits its electrical function: when a fault occurs on the transmission line, ground fault current (potentially thousands of amps for milliseconds) flows through OPGW's metallic strands to the tower ground system — those strands must be sized to absorb that thermal energy pulse without the inner temperature rising enough to damage the fiber core
Fault current sizing is irrelevant to OPGW design; only mechanical tensile strength matters
OPGW's metallic strands exist purely for cosmetic/branding purposes and carry no functional load
pool.explanation: Because OPGW takes over the shield wire's electrical role in the transmission structure, it must also handle that role's electrical consequence — carrying substantial ground fault current during a fault event. The metallic strand sizing (the 'fault current rating') is specifically engineered to absorb that thermal pulse without damaging the embedded fiber, a design requirement that has no equivalent in a purely dielectric cable like ADSS.

pool.prompt: Your company is leasing fiber strands inside an electric utility's OPGW for a 12-mile backbone segment (an IRU arrangement). As the OSP designer, what is your primary responsibility for the OPGW portion of the design?
choices: Designing the OPGW cable's fault current rating and metallic strand sizing
Designing the OPGW's grounding scheme at each transmission structure

The fiber network side: strand count, optical loss budget over the 12-mile segment, and where you'll splice or hand off to your own distribution network — the OPGW's structural design, fault-current sizing, and grounding remain the utility's responsibility, since attachment/lease agreements for OPGW are handled at the utility-to-utility level, not the pole-attachment level
Nothing — leasing OPGW fiber requires no design input from the OSP designer at all
pool.explanation: When leasing fiber strands within someone else's OPGW, the OSP designer's scope is the fiber network layer (strand count, loss budget, splice/handoff points) — the OPGW's structural/electrical engineering (fault current rating, grounding at every structure) remains entirely the owning utility's responsibility, reflecting that OPGW attachment/lease arrangements operate at a different regulatory and contractual level than standard pole attachment.

pool.prompt: Why is ADSS generally preferred over OPGW for joint-use distribution pole attachments?
choices: ADSS has a higher fiber count capacity than OPGW in every case

ADSS is all-dielectric (no metal) — on a joint-use distribution pole, this means the fiber attachment doesn't require grounding hardware, doesn't pick up induced voltages from adjacent phase conductors, and can be safely worked on by communication-space crews without the electrical hazards and grounding requirements OPGW carries. OPGW requires grounding at every structure and carries fault current — appropriate at the top of transmission structures, not in the comm space below a distribution neutral
ADSS is always cheaper than OPGW regardless of application
ADSS and OPGW are functionally interchangeable; the choice is purely aesthetic
pool.explanation: ADSS's defining advantage in a joint-use distribution context is precisely its all-dielectric construction — no grounding hardware needed, no induced-voltage pickup, and safe for comm-space crews to work on without special electrical precautions. OPGW's fault-current-carrying and grounding requirements are appropriate to its transmission-structure role but would be a mismatched, unnecessary electrical hazard if used in the comm space of a distribution pole.

pool.prompt: A design team mistakenly specifies OPGW for a new fiber attachment on a 40-ft joint-use distribution pole corridor, reasoning that 'more robust cable is always better.' What is the actual problem with this choice?
choices: There is no problem — OPGW is simply a superior product in every application

OPGW is engineered for a fundamentally different structural/electrical role (transmission shield wire replacement, fault-current carrying, structure-by-structure grounding) that doesn't apply to a distribution comm-space attachment — specifying it there introduces unnecessary grounding requirements and electrical complexity without any corresponding benefit, since a distribution pole's comm space has no shield-wire function for OPGW to serve
OPGW is illegal to install on any pole shorter than 60 ft
OPGW cannot physically be spliced to any other fiber cable type
pool.explanation: The mismatch isn't about general robustness — it's about applying a product engineered for a specific structural/electrical role (transmission shield-wire replacement with fault-current duty) to a context (distribution comm space) that has no use for that role, while still inheriting its grounding/electrical complexity. 'More robust' doesn't mean 'better fit' when the extra robustness serves a function the application doesn't need.

pool.prompt: Why does an IRU (Indefeasible Right of Use) arrangement for OPGW fiber strands involve a different contractual structure than a standard pole attachment agreement?
choices: There is no real difference; IRU and pole attachment agreements are legally identical

OPGW is embedded within a structural/electrical component of the transmission system itself (the shield wire), owned and operated at the utility-to-utility or carrier-to-utility level — leasing fiber strands inside it is fundamentally different from attaching a separate cable to a pole under standard FCC pole-attachment rules, which is why OPGW fiber leasing uses its own contractual framework (the IRU) rather than the pole-attachment application process covered in T05.L08/L09
IRU arrangements are only used for underground conduit, never for aerial cable of any kind
IRU arrangements eliminate the need for any optical loss budget calculation
pool.explanation: Because OPGW is structurally and electrically integrated into the transmission system itself (rather than being a separate attachment to an existing pole), leasing fiber capacity within it operates under a different contractual model (the IRU) than the pole-attachment application process — this distinction is why T05.L11 treats OPGW fiber leasing as a separate topic from the joint-use/OTMR pole-attachment material in T05.L08/L09.

pool.prompt: Match each aerial cable type to its typical structural context.

items.label: Replaces the overhead shield wire at the top of a transmission tower; carries fault current
All-dielectric; standard choice for joint-use distribution pole attachment
Requires a separate messenger strand; conventional distribution-pole installation method

pool.explanation: Each cable type has a distinct structural niche: OPGW belongs at the top of transmission towers as a shield-wire replacement carrying fault current, ADSS is the standard all-dielectric choice for joint-use distribution pole attachment where grounding-free simplicity matters, and lashed cable is the conventional method requiring its own separate messenger strand on distribution poles.

pool.prompt: A utility offers to lease OPGW fiber strands to your company along a 12-mile transmission corridor, with the utility handling all structural/electrical aspects. Your company's engineering team still needs to verify one thing before committing to the lease: the optical loss budget over the full 12-mile segment. Why is this verification necessary even though the utility owns and maintains the physical cable?
choices: It isn't necessary — the utility's ownership of the physical cable guarantees the fiber network performance will automatically meet any requirement

Because the OSP designer's responsibility (per T05.L11) is specifically the fiber NETWORK side — strand count, splice/handoff points, and the optical loss budget over the leased segment — regardless of who owns the physical cable, the leasing company still needs to confirm the fiber's actual optical performance meets their network's requirements before committing traffic to that path
Loss budget only matters for underground fiber, never for aerial OPGW
The utility is legally required to guarantee zero loss on any leased fiber segment
pool.explanation: Ownership of the physical cable and responsibility for the fiber's actual optical performance are separate concerns — even though the utility handles OPGW's structural/electrical engineering, the leasing company (the OSP designer) still owns the fiber-network-layer verification (loss budget, splice points) since that's what determines whether the leased strands will actually support the intended traffic, which is exactly the division of responsibility established in Q3.
